## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The Profile is NIST's response to Section 4.1.a of Executive Order 14110, which tasked NIST with "developing a companion resource to the Secure Software Development Framework to incorporate secure development practices for generative AI and for dual-use foundation models" [V] [BT]; "This document is that companion resource." [V] (p. 1). It augments the practices and tasks of SSDF version 1.1 (NIST SP 800-218) with recommendations, considerations, notes and informative references specific to generative AI and dual-use foundation model development, documented as an SSDF Community Profile, "a baseline of SSDF practices and tasks that have been enhanced to address a particular use case" [V] (p. 1) [AP]. The abstract describes the additions as practices, tasks, recommendations, considerations, notes and informative references specific to AI model development throughout the software development life cycle (p. i) [AP]. The Profile supplements SP 800-218 and "should not be used without SP 800-218" [V] (p. 1).

The case for a separate profile is that AI models and systems "inherit much of the same risk as any other digital system" [V] but bring new risk too (p. 1) [AR]. "A unique challenge for this community is the blurring of traditional boundaries between system code and system data, as well as the use of plain human language as the means of interaction with the systems." [V] (p. 1). Models, their configuration parameters (e.g., model weights) and the data they interact with (e.g., training data, user queries) "can form closed loops that can be manipulated for unintended functionality" [V] (p. 1) [AR]. "AI model and system development is still much more of an art than an exact science" [V], with developers working on model code, training data and other parameters over multiple iterations; training datasets may come from unknown, untrusted sources; weights and other training parameters can be tampered with; some models may be too complex to inspect thoroughly with ease, which may allow undetectable execution of arbitrary code; and user queries can be crafted to produce undesirable or objectionable output or, if not sanitised, used for injection-style attacks (p. 1) [AR]. "The goal of this document is to identify the practices and tasks needed to address these novel risks." [V] (p. 1).

The Profile is meant for AI model producers, AI system producers and AI system acquirers (p. ii) [AP]. It is "not a checklist to follow" [V] but a starting point for a risk-based approach, to be adapted and customised, since "not all practices and tasks are applicable to all use cases" [V] (p. 4) [AR]. Responsibility for its practices may be shared among organisations, and it addresses only cybersecurity risk, and other risks (e.g., privacy, intellectual property, bias) should be managed along with cybersecurity risk as part of a mature enterprise risk management programme (pp. 4–5) [AR].

The substance is Table 1 (pp. 8–19): each SSDF practice and task, a suggested priority (High, Medium or Low), the AI-specific recommendations, considerations and notes (the table labels them R, C and N), and informative references to the AI RMF 1.0, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications Version 1.1, and NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy (pp. 6–7) [AP]. One practice is new, PW.3, confirming the integrity of training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data before use; its three tasks and three others (PO.5.3, PS.1.2, PS.1.3) are also new (pp. 11–12, 14–15) [AP]. Among the additions: bring AI models, model weights, pipelines and reward models into secure code storage, and protect training data and weights from unauthorised access and modification (PS.1); track provenance of models and data (PS.3.2, PW.3.2); scan and test AI models under code review and testing policies (PW.7, PW.8, RV.1.2); log, monitor and analyse model inputs and outputs (PW.5.1, RV.1.1); consider a human in the loop at named points (PO.4.1, PW.1.1, PW.3.1) and involve one in ongoing scanning and testing as needed (RV.1.2); and set criteria for when to stop using a model and roll back (RV.2.2) [AP].

## Part I: Purpose, scope and use of the Profile

### Front matter (PDF pp. 1–4, pp. i–iv)

The title page names the six authors and their divisions (PDF p. 2) [AP]. The publication was developed under NIST's statutory responsibilities under the Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA) of 2014, and is consistent with OMB Circular A-130 (PDF p. 3) [AP]. Additional information, related content, potential updates and document history are at https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/a/final; contact is ssdf@nist.gov (PDF p. 4) [AP]. The keywords include artificial intelligence model, cybersecurity risk management, generative artificial intelligence, secure software development, software acquisition and software security (p. i) [AP].

The Note to Readers asks standards developing organisations that define secure practices for AI model development and want to map their standard to the SSDF profile to contact the authors, who will introduce them to the National Online Informative References Program (OLIR); the authors welcome feedback on any part of the document, including suggestions for Implementation Examples and Informative References (p. ii) [AP]. The Acknowledgments say that, in response to EO 14110, NIST held a January 2024 workshop where speakers and attendees suggested how to adapt secure software development practices and tasks to the unique aspects of AI model development (p. ii) [AP]. The Patent Disclosure Notice says that, as of publication and following calls for their identification, no patent claims whose use may be required for compliance with the publication's guidance or requirements had been identified to ITL; holders of patents are not obliged to respond to ITL's calls, ITL has not undertaken a patent search, and ITL makes no representation that licences are not required to avoid patent infringement in using the publication (p. iii) [AP].

### Why a profile for AI model development (p. 1)

See the thesis. The risks the Introduction names are the code/data boundary blurring, plain-language interaction, manipulable closed loops among models, parameters and data, iterative art-not-science development, training data from unknown or untrusted sources, tamperable weights and parameters, some models that may be so complex that they cannot easily be thoroughly inspected, and crafted queries leading to objectionable output or injection-style attacks (p. 1) [AR].

### Purpose and relation to SSDF 1.1 (p. 1)

The SSDF provides a common language for describing secure software development practices throughout the software development life cycle (p. 1) [AP]. An example of an addition the Profile makes is: "Secure code storage should include AI models, model weights, pipelines, reward models, and any other AI model elements that need their confidentiality, integrity, and/or availability protected." [V] (p. 1). Readers should also use the implementation examples and informative references in SP 800-218, which are also generally applicable to AI model and AI system development (p. 1) [AP].

### Scope (p. 2)

The scope is AI model development: data sourcing for, designing, training, fine-tuning and evaluating AI models, and incorporating and integrating AI models into other software (p. 2) [AP]. Consistent with SSDF version 1.1 and EO 14110, "practices for the deployment and operation of AI systems with AI models are out of scope" [V] (p. 2). Cybersecurity practices for training data and other data used in AI model development are in scope; the rest of the data governance and management life cycle is out of scope (p. 2) [AP]. The note above Table 1 restates this as most parts of the data governance and management life cycle being out of scope (p. 8) [AP].

The Profile does not distinguish between human-written and AI-generated source code, "because it is assumed that all source code should be evaluated for vulnerabilities and other issues before use" [V] (p. 2) [AR].

### Sources of expertise (p. 2)

The document draws on four sources of expertise (p. 2) [BT]: NIST research and publications on trustworthy and responsible AI (the AI RMF 1.0, the adversarial machine learning taxonomy, the bias standard SP 1270, and the Dioptra experimentation testbed for security evaluations of machine learning algorithms); the SSDF version 1.1, described as a set of fundamental, sound and secure software development practices that gives stakeholders, including producers and acquirers, a common language, and that has been used in support of EO 14028 to enhance software supply chain security; NIST general cybersecurity resources (CSF 2.0, SP 800-53, and the cybersecurity supply chain risk management practices); and AI model developers, AI researchers, AI system developers and secure software practitioners from industry and government, captured mainly through the January 2024 workshop.

### Audiences (p. ii)

There are three primary audiences (p. ii) [AP]:
- AI model producers: organisations developing their own generative AI and dual-use foundation models, as defined in EO 14110;
- AI system producers: organisations developing software that leverages a generative AI or dual-use foundation model;
- AI system acquirers: organisations acquiring a product or service that uses one or more AI systems.

The terms "producer" and "acquirer" were chosen for consistency with the Audience statement of SP 800-218 (p. ii, n. 1) [AP]. Individuals interested in secure development practices for AI models may also benefit. Readers are not expected to be experts in secure software development or AI model development, though such expertise may be needed to implement the practices (p. ii) [AP].

### What the SSDF gives each audience (p. 4)

The three audiences and others can use the SSDF to foster communication about secure AI model development across the life cycle (p. 4) [AP]. Following SSDF practices should help AI model producers reduce the number of vulnerabilities in their models, reduce the potential impact of exploiting undetected or unaddressed vulnerabilities, and "address the root causes of vulnerabilities to prevent recurrences" [V] (p. 4) [AR]. AI system producers can use the SSDF's common vocabulary when talking with AI model producers about their practices and when integrating models into their own software; AI system acquirers can use SSDF terms to "better communicate their cybersecurity requirements and needs" [V] to model and system producers, for example during acquisition (p. 4) [AP]. The document uses a general software development life cycle for consistency with SSDF 1.1, and encourages organisations to adapt it to any machine learning-specific life cycle they use (p. 4, n. 2) [AP].

### A risk-based starting point, not a checklist (p. 4)

"The SSDF Community Profile is not a checklist to follow, but rather a starting point for planning and implementing a risk-based approach to adopting secure software development practices involving AI models." [V] (p. 4). Its contents are meant to be adapted and customised (p. 4) [AP]. Organisations should take a risk-based approach to deciding which practices and tasks are relevant, appropriate and effective against the threats to software development practices, from their own position as AI model producer, AI system producer or AI system acquirer, weighing risk, cost, feasibility and applicability in deciding which to use and how much time and resource to give each (p. 4) [AR]. "Cost models may need to be updated to effectively consider the costs inherent to AI model development." [V] (p. 4). A risk-based approach may change over time as an organisation responds to new or elevated capabilities and risks associated with an AI model or system (p. 4) [AR].

### Model versioning and lineage (p. 4)

Generative AI and dual-use foundation models make versioning and lineage harder to track (p. 4) [AR]. Source code that defines a model's architecture and builds its binaries is amenable to secure software engineering practices for versioning, lineage and reproducibility; but "the final model weights are defined only after the model is trained and fine-tuned" [V], and that is where limits in tracking every aspect of collection, processing and training arise (p. 4) [AR]. Organisations should follow secure development practices for the parts of a model that can be covered fully and strive to bring in secure practices as far as possible where security guarantees are hard to achieve; "Organizations should document the parts and artifacts that are not covered by the secure software development practices." [V] (p. 4).

The Profile's practices, tasks, recommendations and considerations can be integrated into machine learning operations (MLOps) along with other software assets in a continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline (p. 4) [AP].

### Shared responsibility (pp. 4–5)

Responsibility for implementing the Profile's practices may be shared among organisations: a model produced by one organisation may run inside an AI system hosted by a second and be used by others (p. 4) [AE]. In such cases "there is likely a shared responsibility model" [V] involving the AI model producer, AI system producer and AI system acquirer (p. 5). An acquirer can establish an agreement with a system producer and/or model producer specifying "which party is responsible for each practice and task and how each party will attest to its conformance with the agreement" [V] (p. 5) [AP].

### A limitation: cybersecurity risk only (p. 5)

"A limitation of the SSDF and this Profile is that they only address cybersecurity risk management." [V] (p. 5). Other risks to AI systems (e.g., data privacy, intellectual property and bias) should be managed alongside cybersecurity risk as part of a mature enterprise risk management programme (p. 5) [AR]. The NIST resources listed for those risks are the AI RMF and the AI RMF Playbook; the adversarial machine learning taxonomy; the AI RMF Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile; the bias standard; the cybersecurity supply chain risk management practices; the NIST Privacy Framework, Version 1.0; and Integrating Cybersecurity and Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) (p. 5) [BT].

## Part II: How Table 1 is built (pp. 6–8)

### Columns, tags and identifiers (p. 6)

Table 1 has five columns (p. 6) [AP]. *Practice* gives the practice's name and unique identifier and a brief explanation of what it is and why it helps. *Task* gives one or more actions that may be needed to perform the practice, each with a unique identifier. All practices and tasks are unchanged from SSDF version 1.1 unless tagged "Modified from SSDF 1.1" or "Not part of SSDF 1.1"; the example given is the PW.3 practice, "Confirm the Integrity of Training, Testing, Fine-Tuning, and Aligning Data Before Use" [V], and all its tasks (p. 6).

*Recommendations, Considerations, and Notes Specific to AI Model Development* holds items that recommend what to do or describe further considerations for a task; organisations are expected to adapt, customise and omit items as part of the risk-based approach (p. 6) [AP]. Each item's ID starts with "R" for a recommendation ("something the organization should do" [V]), "C" for a consideration ("something the organization should consider doing" [V]) or "N" for a note ("additional information besides recommendations and considerations" [V]) (p. 6). An R, C or N designation and its number appended to the task ID gives a unique identifier, e.g. PO.1.2.R1 for the first recommendation of task PO.1.2 (p. 6) [AP]. "No additions to SSDF 1.1" in this column means the Profile has no AI-specific recommendations, considerations or notes for the task; readers should go to SSDF version 1.1 for baseline guidance and to the other references for more (p. 6) [AP].

*Informative References* map to parts of standards, guidance and other content with requirements, recommendations, considerations or other information on performing the task (pp. 6–7) [AP].

### Priority (p. 6)

Priority reflects the suggested relative importance of each task within the profile and "is intended to be a starting point for organizations to assign their own priorities" [V] (p. 6). The three levels (p. 6):
- High: "Critically important for AI model development security compared to other tasks" [V];
- Medium: "Directly supports AI model development security" [V];
- Low: "Beneficial for secure software development but is generally not more important than most other tasks" [V].

### Informative reference sources (p. 7)

The informative references come from three sources (p. 7) [BT]: the AI Risk Management Framework 1.0, for which several crosswalks to other guidance and standards are listed at https://airc.nist.gov/AI_RMF_Knowledge_Base/Crosswalks; the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications Version 1.1, where each identifier indicates one of the top 10 vulnerability types and may also refer to an individual prevention and mitigation strategy for that type; and Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, which outlines key types of machine learning attack stages and attacker goals, objectives and capabilities, with corresponding mitigation methods. In Table 1 these appear under the labels "AI RMF:", "OWASP:" and "Adv ML" (pp. 8–19) [AP]. The AI RMF entries are given as a name and number (Govern, Map, Measure or Manage, e.g. "Map 1.3"); the OWASP entries are given as identifiers only (e.g. LLM05, LLM05-1, LLM03-7d), and the Profile does not name the vulnerability types or strategies they stand for (pp. 8–19) [AP].

### Implementation Examples and numbering gaps (pp. 7–8)

NIST is considering adding an Implementation Examples column in a future version (p. 7) [AP]. An Implementation Example is "a single sentence that suggests a way to accomplish part or all of a task" [V]; the Recommendations and Considerations column describes the "what", Implementation Examples would give options for the "how", supplementing those already in SSDF version 1.1 (p. 7) [AP].

Some SSDF practice and task numbers have gaps: the PW.4 practice has three tasks, PW.4.1, PW.4.2 and PW.4.4, because PW.4.3 was a task in SSDF version 1.0 that moved elsewhere in version 1.1 and its ID was not reused (p. 8) [AP].

## Part III: Prepare the Organization (PO) (pp. 8–11)

### PO.1, Define Security Requirements for Software Development (p. 8)

The practice: make sure security requirements for software development are known at all times, so they are taken into account throughout the SDLC and collected once and shared; they include internal sources (policies, business objectives, risk management strategy) and external ones (applicable laws and regulations) (PO.1, p. 8) [AP].

- **PO.1.1** (High). Identify and document all security requirements for the organisation's software development infrastructures and processes, and maintain them over time. R1: include AI model development in the security requirements for software development infrastructure and processes. R2: identify and select appropriate AI model architectures and training techniques in line with recommended practices for cybersecurity, privacy and reproducibility. References: AI RMF Map 1.3, 1.5, 1.6 (PO.1.1, p. 8) [AP].
- **PO.1.2** (High). Identify and document all security requirements for organisation-developed software to meet, and maintain them over time. R1: organisational policies should support all current requirements specific to AI model development security for organisation-developed software, covering AI model development, AI model operations and data science; requirements may come from laws, regulations, contracts and standards. C1: "Consider reusing or expanding the organization’s existing data classification policy and processes." [V] N1: "Possible forms of AI model documentation include data, model, and system cards." [V] References: AI RMF Govern 1.1, 1.2, 3.2, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1; Map 1.1 (PO.1.2, p. 8).
- **PO.1.3** (Medium; Modified from SSDF 1.1). Communicate requirements to all third parties who will provide commercial software components to the organisation for use by its own software. R1: include AI model development security in the requirements communicated for third-party software components. References: AI RMF Map 4.1, 4.2; OWASP LLM05-1 (PO.1.3, p. 8) [AP].

### PO.2, Implement Roles and Responsibilities (p. 9)

The practice: make sure everyone inside and outside the organisation involved in the SDLC is prepared to perform their SDLC-related roles and responsibilities (PO.2, p. 9) [AP].

- **PO.2.1** (High). Create new roles and alter responsibilities for existing roles to cover all parts of the SDLC; periodically review, maintain and update them. R1: include AI model development security in SDLC-related roles and responsibilities throughout the SDLC, covering, but not limited to, AI model development, AI model operations and data science. N1: roles and responsibilities involving AI system producers, AI model producers and other third-party providers can be documented in agreements. References: AI RMF Govern 2.1 (PO.2.1, p. 9) [AP].
- **PO.2.2** (High). Provide role-based training for all personnel whose responsibilities contribute to secure development; periodically review proficiency and training and update it. R1: role-based training should include understanding cybersecurity vulnerabilities and threats to AI models and their possible mitigations. References: AI RMF Govern 2.2; OWASP LLM04-7 (PO.2.2, p. 9) [AP].
- **PO.2.3** (Medium). Obtain upper management or authorising official commitment to secure development and convey it to everyone with development-related roles. R1: leadership should commit to secure development practices involving AI models. References: AI RMF Govern 2.3 (PO.2.3, p. 9) [AP].

### PO.3, Implement Supporting Toolchains (pp. 9–10)

The practice: use automation to reduce human effort and improve the accuracy, reproducibility, usability and comprehensiveness of security practices across the SDLC, and to document and demonstrate their use; toolchains may be organisation-wide or project-specific and may address one part of the SDLC, such as a build pipeline (PO.3, p. 9) [AP].

- **PO.3.1** (High). Specify which tools or tool types must or should be in each toolchain to mitigate identified risks, and how the components integrate. R1: plan to develop and implement automated toolchains that secure AI model development and reduce human effort, especially at the scale AI models often use. N1: ideally, automated toolchains will do the vast majority of the work of securing AI model development. N2: see PO.4, PO.5, PS and PW for tool types. References: AI RMF Measure 2.1; OWASP LLM08 (PO.3.1, p. 9) [AP].
- **PO.3.2** (High). Follow recommended security practices to deploy, operate and maintain tools and toolchains. R1: execute the plan to develop and implement those automated toolchains. R2: verify the security of toolchains at a frequency commensurate with risk. References: AI RMF Measure 2.1; OWASP LLM05-3, LLM05-9, LLM08, LLM09 (PO.3.2, p. 9) [AP].
- **PO.3.3** (Medium). Configure tools to generate artifacts of their support of secure software development practices as the organisation defines them. N1 defines an artifact as an item of evidence, citing [16], and evidence, citing [17], as grounds for belief or disbelief, data on which to base proof or establish truth or falsehood [BT]; artifacts provide records of secure development practices, and AI-specific examples include attestations of the integrity and provenance of training datasets. References: AI RMF Measure 2.1 (PO.3.3, p. 10) [AP].

### PO.4, Define and Use Criteria for Software Security Checks (p. 10)

The practice: help make sure the software resulting from the SDLC meets the organisation's expectations by defining and using criteria for checking its security during development (PO.4, p. 10) [AP].

- **PO.4.1** (Medium). Define criteria for software security checks and track them throughout the SDLC. R1: implement guardrails and other controls throughout the AI development life cycle, extending beyond the traditional SDLC. C1: consider requiring review and approval from a human-in-the-loop for software security checks beyond risk-based thresholds. References: AI RMF Measure 2.3, 2.7; Manage 1.1; OWASP LLM01-2 (PO.4.1, p. 10) [AP].
- **PO.4.2** (Low). Implement processes, mechanisms, etc. to gather and safeguard the information the criteria need. No additions to SSDF 1.1. References: AI RMF Measure 2.3, 2.7; Manage 1.1; OWASP LLM01-2 (PO.4.2, p. 10) [AP].

### PO.5, Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development (pp. 10–11)

The practice, tagged "Modified from SSDF 1.1" in the Practice column: make sure every component of the software development environments is strongly protected from internal and external threats, to prevent compromise of the environments or the software developed or maintained in them; example environments are development, AI model training, build, test and distribution (PO.5, p. 10) [AP].

- **PO.5.1** (High). Separate and protect each environment involved in software development. C1, listed first: consider separating execution environments from each other as far as feasible, e.g. by isolation, segmentation, containment or access via APIs. R1: monitor, track and limit resource usage and rates for AI model users during model development. R2: store sensitive data used in AI model development, including production data, only in organisation-approved environments and locations within them. R3: protect all training pipelines, model registries and other components in the environments according to the principle of least privilege. R4: "Continuously monitor training-related activity in pipelines and model modifications in the model registry." [V] R5: follow recommended practices for securely configuring each environment. R6: "Continuously monitor each environment for plaintext secrets." [V] References: OWASP LLM01-1, LLM01-4, LLM04, LLM08, LLM10 (PO.5.1, pp. 10–11).
- **PO.5.2** (Medium). Secure and harden development endpoints (for designers, developers, testers, builders, etc.) using a risk-based approach. No additions to SSDF 1.1. References: OWASP LLM01-1, LLM05-3, LLM05-9, LLM08 (PO.5.2, p. 11) [AP].
- **PO.5.3** (High; Not part of SSDF 1.1). Continuously monitor software execution performance and behaviour in development environments to spot potential suspicious activity and other issues. R1: perform continuous security monitoring of all development environment components that host an AI model or related resources (e.g., model APIs, weights, configuration parameters, training datasets). R2: monitoring and analysis tools should generate alerts when activity involving an AI model passes a risk threshold or otherwise merits investigation. References: AI RMF Measure 2.4; OWASP LLM03-7, LLM04, LLM05-8, LLM09, LLM10 (PO.5.3, p. 11) [AP].

## Part IV: Protect Software (PS) (pp. 11–13)

### PS.1, Protect All Forms of Code and Data from Unauthorized Access and Tampering (pp. 11–12)

The practice, tagged "Modified from SSDF 1.1" in the Practice column: help prevent unauthorised changes to code and data, inadvertent or intentional, that could circumvent or negate the software's intended security characteristics; for code and data not meant to be public, this helps prevent theft and may make it harder or slower for attackers to find vulnerabilities (PS.1, p. 11) [AP].

- **PS.1.1** (High). Store all forms of code (source, executable, configuration-as-code) on the principle of least privilege, so only authorised personnel, tools, services, etc. have access. R1: secure code storage should include AI models, model weights, pipelines, reward models and any other AI model elements whose confidentiality, integrity and/or availability need protecting; they need not all be stored in the same place or by the same mechanism. R2: follow least privilege to minimise direct access to AI models and model elements wherever they are stored or executed. R3: store reward models separately from AI models and data. R4: "Permit indirect access only to model weights." [V] C1: "Consider preventing all human access to model weights." [V] C2: consider requiring all AI model development to be done in organisation-approved environments only. References: OWASP LLM10 (PS.1.1, pp. 11–12).
- **PS.1.2** (High; Not part of SSDF 1.1). Protect all training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data from unauthorised access and modification. R1: continuously monitor the confidentiality (for non-public data only) and integrity of that data. C1: consider storing that data securely for future use and reference, if feasible. References: OWASP LLM03, LLM06, LLM10 (PS.1.2, p. 12) [AP].
- **PS.1.3** (High; Not part of SSDF 1.1). Protect all model weights and configuration parameter data from unauthorised access and modification. R1: keep model weights and configuration parameters separate from training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data. R2: continuously monitor the confidentiality (for closed models only) and integrity of weights and configuration parameters. R3: follow least privilege to restrict access to weights, configuration parameters and services during development. R4: "Specify and implement additional risk-proportionate cybersecurity practices around model weights, such as encryption, cryptographic hashes, digital signatures, multi-party authorization, and air-gapped environments." [V] References: OWASP LLM10 (PS.1.3, p. 12).

### PS.2, Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity (p. 12)

The practice: help acquirers make sure the software they acquire is legitimate and untampered (PS.2, p. 12) [AP].

- **PS.2.1** (Medium). Make software integrity verification information available to acquirers. R1: generate and provide cryptographic hashes or digital signatures for an AI model and its components, artifacts and documentation. R2: provide digital signatures for AI model changes. References: OWASP LLM05-6 (PS.2.1, p. 12) [AP].

### PS.3, Archive and Protect Each Software Release (pp. 12–13)

The practice: preserve software releases to help identify, analyse and eliminate vulnerabilities found after release (PS.3, pp. 12–13) [AP].

- **PS.3.1** (Low). Securely archive the files and supporting data (e.g., integrity verification information, provenance data) to be retained for each release. R1: version and track infrastructure tools (e.g., pre-processing, transforms, collection) that support dataset creation and model training. R2: include documentation of the justification for AI model selection in the retained information. R3: include documentation of the entire training process, such as data preprocessing and model architecture. N1: "AI models and their components may need to be added at this time to an organization’s asset inventories." [V] References: OWASP LLM10 (PS.3.1, pp. 12–13).
- **PS.3.2** (Medium; Modified from SSDF 1.1). Collect, safeguard, maintain and share provenance data for all components of each release (e.g., in a software bill of materials [SBOM], through Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts [SLSA]). R1: track the provenance of an AI model and its components and derivatives, including the training libraries, frameworks and pipelines used to build it. R2: track AI models trained on sensitive data (e.g., payment card data, protected health information, other personally identifiable information), and decide whether access to those models should be restricted to people who already have access to that training data. C1: consider disclosing the provenance of the training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data used for a model. References: OWASP LLM03-1, LLM05-4, LLM05-5, LLM10 (PS.3.2, p. 13) [AP].

## Part V: Produce Well-Secured Software (PW) (pp. 13–17)

### PW.1, Design Software to Meet Security Requirements and Mitigate Security Risks (pp. 13–14)

The practice: identify and evaluate the software's security requirements; determine what security risks it is likely to face in operation and how its design and architecture should mitigate them; and justify any case where risk-based analysis says requirements should be relaxed or waived. Addressing security requirements and risks during design (secure by design) is key to improving software security and also helps development efficiency (PW.1, pp. 13–14) [AP].

- **PW.1.1** (High). Use forms of risk modelling, such as threat modelling, attack modelling or attack surface mapping, to help assess the software's security risk. R1: incorporate relevant AI model-specific vulnerability and threat types in risk modelling; the examples, citing [3], are poisoning of training data, malicious code or other unwanted content in inputs and outputs, denial-of-service conditions arising from adversarial prompts, supply chain attacks, unauthorised information disclosure, theft of AI model weights, and misconfiguration of data pipelines [BT]. C1: consider periodic risk modelling updates for future model versions and derivatives after release. C2: during risk modelling, consider checking that the AI model is not on a critical path for making significant security decisions without a human in the loop [AP]. References: AI RMF Govern 4.1, 4.2; Map 5.1; Measure 1.1; Manage 1.2, 1.3; OWASP LLM01, LLM02, LLM03, LLM04, LLM05, LLM06, LLM07, LLM08, LLM09, LLM10 (PW.1.1, pp. 13–14).
- **PW.1.2** (Medium). Track and maintain the software's security requirements, risks and design decisions. No additions to SSDF 1.1. References: AI RMF Govern 4.1, 4.2; Map 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 3.2, 3.3, 4.1, 4.2, 5.2; Manage 1.2, 1.3, 1.4 (PW.1.2, p. 14) [AP].
- **PW.1.3** (Medium). Where appropriate, build in support for standardised security features and services (e.g., integrating with existing log management, identity management, access control and vulnerability management systems) instead of proprietary implementations. No additions to SSDF 1.1; no informative references (PW.1.3, p. 14) [AP].

### PW.2, Review the Software Design to Verify Compliance with Security Requirements and Risk Information (p. 14)

The practice: help make sure the software will meet the security requirements and satisfactorily address the identified risk information (PW.2, p. 14) [AP].

- **PW.2.1** (High; Modified from SSDF 1.1). Have 1) a qualified person or people not involved with the design and 2) automated processes instantiated in the toolchain review the design to confirm and enforce that it meets all security requirements and satisfactorily addresses the identified risk information. No additions to SSDF 1.1. References: AI RMF Measure 2.7; Manage 1.1 (PW.2.1, p. 14) [AP].

### PW.3, Confirm the Integrity of Training, Testing, Fine-Tuning, and Aligning Data Before Use (pp. 14–15)

The practice, tagged "Not part of SSDF 1.1" in the Practice column: prevent data likely to harm the cybersecurity of the AI model from being consumed in its training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning (PW.3, pp. 14–15) [AP].

- **PW.3.1** (High; Not part of SSDF 1.1). Analyse data for signs of data poisoning, bias, homogeneity and tampering before using it to train, test, fine-tune or align an AI model, and mitigate the risks as necessary. R1: verify the provenance (when known) and integrity of that data before use. R2: select and apply appropriate methods for analysing and altering it; the examples are anomaly detection, bias detection, data cleaning, data curation, data filtering, data sanitisation, fact-checking and noise reduction. C1: consider using a human-in-the-loop to examine data, such as with exploratory data analysis techniques, citing [18] [BT]. References: AI RMF Measure 2.1; Manage 1.2, 1.3; OWASP LLM03, LLM06 (PW.3.1, pp. 14–15) [AP].
- **PW.3.2** (Medium; Not part of SSDF 1.1). Track the provenance, when known, of all training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data used for a model, and document which data lack known provenance. N1: provenance verification is not possible in every case because provenance is not always known, but it is still beneficial for security to track and verify provenance whenever possible and to track when it is unknown. References: AI RMF Measure 2.1; OWASP LLM03-1; Adv ML (PW.3.2, p. 15) [AP].
- **PW.3.3** (Medium; Not part of SSDF 1.1). Include adversarial samples in the training and testing data to improve attack prevention. R1: use a process and corresponding controls to test the adversarial samples and put appropriate guardrails on their training and testing use. References: OWASP LLM03-6, LLM05-7; Adv ML (PW.3.3, p. 15) [AP].

### PW.4, Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software When Feasible Instead of Duplicating Functionality (pp. 15–16)

The practice: lower development cost, speed development and reduce the chance of introducing new vulnerabilities by reusing modules and services whose security posture has already been checked; this matters most for software that implements security functionality, such as cryptographic modules and protocols (PW.4, p. 15) [AP].

- **PW.4.1** (Medium). Acquire and maintain well-secured software components (e.g., libraries, modules, middleware, frameworks) from commercial, open-source and other third-party developers. C1: consider using an existing AI model instead of creating a new one. References: OWASP LLM05 (PW.4.1, p. 15) [AP].
- **PW.4.2** (Low). Create and maintain well-secured components in-house, following SDLC processes, for common internal needs third-party components cannot better meet. No additions to SSDF 1.1; no informative references (PW.4.2, p. 15) [AP].
- **PW.4.4** (High). Verify that acquired commercial, open-source and other third-party components comply with the organisation's requirements throughout their life cycles. R1: verify the integrity, provenance and security of an existing AI model or any other acquired AI components (training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning datasets; reward models; adaptation layers; configuration parameters) before using them. R2: scan and thoroughly test acquired AI models and their components for vulnerabilities and malicious content before use. References: OWASP LLM05-2, LLM05-6; Adv ML (PW.4.4, pp. 15–16) [AP].

### PW.5, Create Source Code by Adhering to Secure Coding Practices (p. 16)

The practice: decrease the number of security vulnerabilities in the software, and reduce costs by minimising vulnerabilities introduced during source code creation that meet or exceed organisation-defined severity criteria (PW.5, p. 16) [AP].

- **PW.5.1** (High). Follow all secure coding practices appropriate to the development languages and environment to meet the organisation's requirements. R1: expand secure coding practices to include AI technology-specific considerations. R2: code the handling of inputs (including prompts and user data) and outputs carefully; all inputs and outputs should be logged, analysed and validated within the context of the AI model, and those with issues should be sanitised or dropped. R3: encode inputs and outputs to prevent the execution of unauthorised code. References: AI RMF Manage 1.2, 1.3, 1.4; OWASP LLM01, LLM02, LLM04-1, LLM06, LLM07, LLM09-9, LLM10 (PW.5.1, p. 16) [AP].

### PW.6, Configure the Compilation, Interpreter, and Build Processes to Improve Executable Security (p. 16)

The practice: decrease vulnerabilities and reduce costs by eliminating vulnerabilities before testing (PW.6, p. 16) [AP].

- **PW.6.1** (Low). Use compiler, interpreter and build tools that offer features to improve executable security. C1: consider using secure model serialisation mechanisms that reduce or eliminate vectors for introducing malicious content. No informative references (PW.6.1, p. 16) [AP].
- **PW.6.2** (Low). Decide which compiler, interpreter and build tool features to use and how to configure each, then implement and use the approved configurations. C1: consider capturing compiler, interpreter and build tool versions and features as part of provenance tracking. No informative references (PW.6.2, p. 16) [AP].

### PW.7, Review and/or Analyze Human-Readable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements (pp. 16–17)

The practice: help find vulnerabilities so they can be corrected before release, to prevent exploitation; automated methods lower the effort and resources needed; human-readable code includes source code, scripts and any other code the organisation deems human-readable (PW.7, p. 16) [AP].

- **PW.7.1** (Medium). Decide whether code review (a person looks directly at the code) and/or code analysis (tools find issues, fully automated or with a person) should be used, as the organisation defines. R1: code review and analysis policies or guidelines should include code for AI models and related components. C1: consider performing scans of AI model code in addition to testing the AI models. No informative references (PW.7.1, p. 16) [AP].
- **PW.7.2** (High). Perform the code review and/or analysis against the organisation's secure coding standards, and record and triage all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the development team's workflow or issue tracking system. R1: scan all AI models for malware, vulnerabilities, backdoors and other security issues in line with the organisation's code review and analysis policies or guidelines. References: AI RMF Measure 2.3, 2.7; Manage 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4; OWASP LLM03-7d, LLM07-4 (PW.7.2, pp. 16–17) [AP].

### PW.8, Test Executable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements (p. 17)

The practice: help find vulnerabilities so they can be corrected before release; automated methods lower effort and resources and improve traceability and repeatability; executable code includes binaries, directly executed bytecode and source code, and any other code the organisation deems executable (PW.8, p. 17) [AP].

- **PW.8.1** (High). Decide whether executable code testing should be done to find vulnerabilities that earlier reviews, analysis or testing missed and, if so, which types. R1: include AI models in code testing policies and guidelines; forms of code testing usable for AI models include unit testing, integration testing, penetration testing, red teaming, use case testing and adversarial testing. C1: consider automating tests within a development pipeline as part of regression testing where possible. No informative references (PW.8.1, p. 17) [AP].
- **PW.8.2** (High). Scope the testing, design the tests, perform them and document the results, including recording and triaging all discovered issues and recommended remediations in the development team's workflow or issue tracking system. R1: test all AI models for vulnerabilities in line with the organisation's code testing policies or guidelines. R2: retest AI models when they are retrained or new data sources are added. References: AI RMF Measure 2.2, 2.3, 2.7; Manage 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4; OWASP LLM03-7d, LLM05-7, LLM07-4 (PW.8.2, p. 17) [AP].

### PW.9, Configure Software to Have Secure Settings by Default (p. 17)

The practice: improve security at installation, to reduce the chance of the software being deployed with weak security settings and put at greater risk of compromise (PW.9, p. 17) [AP].

- **PW.9.1** (Medium). Define a secure baseline by deciding how to configure each security-affecting or security-related setting so the defaults are secure and do not weaken the security functions of the platform, network infrastructure or services. No additions to SSDF 1.1. References: AI RMF Measure 2.7 (PW.9.1, p. 17) [AP].
- **PW.9.2** (Medium). Implement the default settings (or groups of them) and document each setting for software administrators. N1: settings can be documented earlier, such as when defining the secure baseline (see PW.9.1). References: AI RMF Measure 2.7; Manage 1.2, 1.3, 1.4 (PW.9.2, p. 17) [AP].

## Part VI: Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV) (pp. 17–19)

### RV.1, Identify and Confirm Vulnerabilities on an Ongoing Basis (pp. 17–18)

The practice: help identify vulnerabilities more quickly so they can be remediated more quickly in line with risk, shrinking attackers' window of opportunity (RV.1, pp. 17–18) [AP].

- **RV.1.1** (High). Gather information from acquirers, users and public sources on potential vulnerabilities in the software and the third-party components it uses, and investigate all credible reports. R1: log, monitor and analyse all inputs and outputs for AI models to detect possible security and performance issues (see PO.5.3). R2: make users of AI models aware of mechanisms for reporting potential security and performance issues. N1: in this context, "users" means AI system producers and acquirers who are using an AI model. R3: monitor vulnerability and incident databases for information on AI-related concerns, including the machine learning frameworks and libraries used to build AI models. References: AI RMF Govern 4.3, 5.1, 6.1, 6.2; Measure 1.2, 2.4, 2.5, 2.7, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3; Manage 4.1; OWASP LLM03-7a, LLM09, LLM10 (RV.1.1, pp. 17–18) [AP].
- **RV.1.2** (Medium). Review, analyse and/or test the software's code to identify or confirm previously undetected vulnerabilities. R1: scan and test AI models frequently to find previously undetected vulnerabilities. R2: rely mainly on automation for ongoing scanning and testing, and involve a human-in-the-loop as needed. R3: conduct periodic audits of AI models. References: AI RMF Govern 4.3; Measure 1.3, 2.4, 2.7, 3.1; Manage 4.1; OWASP LLM03-7b, LLM03-7d (RV.1.2, p. 18) [AP].
- **RV.1.3** (Medium). Have a policy for vulnerability disclosure and remediation, and implement the roles, responsibilities and processes to support it. R1: include AI model vulnerabilities in organisation vulnerability disclosure and remediation policies. R2: make users of AI models aware of their inherent limitations and how to report any cybersecurity problems they meet. References: AI RMF Govern 4.3, 5.1, 6.1; Measure 3.1, 3.3; Manage 4.3 (RV.1.3, p. 18) [AP].

### RV.2, Assess, Prioritize, and Remediate Vulnerabilities (pp. 18–19)

The practice: help make sure vulnerabilities are remediated in line with risk, shrinking attackers' window of opportunity (RV.2, p. 18) [AP].

- **RV.2.1** (Medium). Analyse each vulnerability to gather enough information about its risk to plan its remediation or other risk response. N1: this may include deep analysis of generative AI and dual-use foundation model input and output to detect deviations from normal behaviour. References: AI RMF Govern 4.3, 5.1, 6.1; Measure 2.7, 3.1; Manage 1.2, 2.3, 4.1; Adv ML (RV.2.1, p. 18) [AP].
- **RV.2.2** (High). Plan and implement risk responses for vulnerabilities. R1: risk responses for AI models should consider the time and expense that rebuilding them may involve. R2: establish and implement criteria and processes for when to stop using an AI model and when to roll back to a previous version and its components. C1: "Consider being prepared to stop using an AI model at any time and to continue operations through other means until the AI model’s risks are sufficiently addressed." [V] References: AI RMF Govern 5.1, 5.2, 6.1; Measure 3.3; Manage 1.3, 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 4.1 (RV.2.2, pp. 18–19).

### RV.3, Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes (p. 19)

The practice: help reduce the frequency of vulnerabilities in future (RV.3, p. 19) [AP].

- **RV.3.1** (Medium). Analyse identified vulnerabilities to determine their root causes. N1: being able to review training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data after the fact can help identify some root causes. References: AI RMF Govern 5.1, 6.1; Measure 2.7, 3.1; Manage 2.3, 4.1 (RV.3.1, p. 19) [AP].
- **RV.3.2** (Medium). Analyse root causes over time to find patterns, such as a particular secure coding practice not being followed consistently. No additions to SSDF 1.1. References: AI RMF Govern 5.1, 6.1; Measure 2.7, 3.1; Manage 4.1, 4.3 (RV.3.2, p. 19) [AP].
- **RV.3.3** (Medium). Review the software for similar vulnerabilities to eradicate a class of vulnerabilities, and fix them proactively rather than waiting for external reports. No additions to SSDF 1.1. References: AI RMF Govern 5.1, 5.2, 6.1; Measure 2.7, 3.1; Manage 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 (RV.3.3, p. 19) [AP].
- **RV.3.4** (Medium). Review the SDLC process and update it if appropriate to prevent, or reduce the likelihood of, the root cause recurring in updates to the software or in new software. No additions to SSDF 1.1. References: AI RMF Govern 5.2, 6.1; Measure 2.7, 3.1; Manage 4.2, 4.3 (RV.3.4, p. 19) [AP].

## Part VII: Glossary (p. 22)

Appendix A defines nine terms, each with its source (p. 22) [BT]:
- artificial intelligence: a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments [1];
- artificial intelligence model: a component of an information system that implements AI technology and uses computational, statistical or machine-learning techniques to produce outputs from a given set of inputs [1];
- artificial intelligence red-teaming: "A structured testing effort to find flaws and vulnerabilities in an AI system, often in a controlled environment and in collaboration with developers of AI." [V] [1];
- artificial intelligence system: any data system, software, hardware, application, tool or utility that operates in whole or in part using AI [1];
- data science: the field combining domain expertise, programming skills and knowledge of mathematics and statistics to extract meaningful insights from data [19];
- dual-use foundation model: an AI model trained on broad data; generally using self-supervision; containing "at least tens of billions of parameters" [V]; applicable across a wide range of contexts; and exhibiting, or easily modifiable to exhibit, high performance at tasks posing a serious risk to security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or any combination, such as by substantially lowering the barrier for non-experts to design, synthesise, acquire or use chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear (CBRN) weapons, enabling powerful offensive cyber operations through automated vulnerability discovery and exploitation against a wide range of potential targets of cyber attacks, or permitting the evasion of human control or oversight through deception or obfuscation; models meet the definition even if provided to end users with technical safeguards against those capabilities [1];
- generative artificial intelligence: the class of AI models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data to generate derived synthetic content, which can include images, videos, audio, text and other digital content [1];
- model weight: "A numerical parameter within an AI model that helps determine the model’s outputs in response to inputs." [V] [1];
- provenance: "Metadata pertaining to the origination or source of specified data." [V] [13].

## Connections the author makes in the text

- Executive Order 14110, *Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence* [1]: Section 4.1.a is the tasking the Profile answers; it defines dual-use foundation models for the Audience, and is the source of seven of the nine glossary definitions [BT] (pp. i, ii, 1, 2, 22).
- NIST SP 800-218, *Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1* (Souppaya, Scarfone, Dodson 2022) [6]: the base the Profile supplements and must be used with; its implementation examples and informative references are generally applicable to AI work; the terms "producer" and "acquirer" were chosen for consistency with its Audience statement; SSDF version 1.0 is named for the PW.4.3 numbering gap [BT] (pp. 1, 2, 6, 8, ii).
- NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1) [2]: a source of expertise, a resource for other risks, and one of the three informative-reference sources ("AI RMF:"), with crosswalks to other guidance [BT] (pp. 2, 5, 7).
- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications Version 1.1 (OWASP 2023, https://llmtop10.com) [15]: one of the three informative-reference sources ("OWASP:"), cited by identifier only, e.g. LLM05-1, LLM03-7d [BT] (pp. 7, 8–18).
- *Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations* (Vassilev, Oprea, Fordyce, Anderson 2024; NIST AI 100-2e2023) [3]: a source of expertise, a resource for other risks, one of the three informative-reference sources ("Adv ML"), and the citation for PW.1.1.R1's threat-type examples [BT] (pp. 2, 5, 7, 13).
- NIST SP 1270, *Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence* (Schwartz et al. 2022) [4], and Dioptra [5]: sources of expertise; SP 1270 is also listed for other risks [BT] (pp. 2, 5).
- Executive Order 14028, *Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity* [7]: the SSDF has been used in support of it to enhance software supply chain security [BT] (p. 2).
- NIST CSF 2.0 [8], SP 800-53 Rev. 5 [9] and SP 800-161r1 (Boyens et al. 2022) [10]: general cybersecurity resources drawn on; SP 800-161r1 is also listed for other risks [BT] (pp. 2, 5).
- NIST AI RMF Playbook [11], AI RMF Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1) [12], NIST Privacy Framework Version 1.0 [13] and NIST IR 8286 (Stine et al. 2020) [14]: listed as resources for risks other than cybersecurity; [13] is also the source of the glossary's provenance definition [BT] (pp. 5, 22).
- NIST IR 7692 (OCIL 2.0, Waltermire, Scarfone, Casipe 2011) [16] and NIST SP 800-160v1r1 (Ross, McEvilley, Winstead 2022) [17]: definitions of artifact and evidence in PO.3.3.N1 [BT] (p. 10).
- NIST/SEMATECH *Engineering Statistics Handbook*, "What is EDA?" [18]: exploratory data analysis in PW.3.1.C1 [BT] (p. 15).
- Reznik, *Intelligent Security Systems* (2022) [19]: the glossary's data science definition [BT] (p. 22).
- Software bill of materials (SBOM) and Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA): named as vehicles for provenance data in PS.3.2 [BT] (p. 13).
- FISMA 2014 and OMB Circular A-130: the Authority section [BT] (PDF p. 3).
- National Online Informative References Program (OLIR): where standards bodies can submit mappings to the profile [BT] (p. ii).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *The Profile as a checklist.* It is "not a checklist to follow" but a starting point for a risk-based approach, to be adapted and customised (p. 4).
- *Using the Profile on its own.* It "should not be used without SP 800-218" (p. 1); the note above Table 1 repeats that it is meant to be used with SSDF 1.1, not on its own (p. 8).
- *Treating AI-generated source code differently from human-written code.* The Profile does not distinguish them, because all source code is assumed to need evaluation before use (p. 2).
